author: Talanda Cooper
title: Athletes' strength on display at Central Carolina Highland Games - NewsBreak
text:
By Talanda Cooper ,
1 days ago
Inner strength was on display alongside sheer raw power Saturday at the Central Carolina Highland Games on the campus of Central Children’s Home in Oxford.
Competitors participated in traditional Highland Games competitions such as stone throw and caber toss, and there also were sword fighting matches presented by the Triangle Sword Fighting Guild.
The event raises funds for Central Children’s Home. It attracts top strength athletes from North Carolina and beyond.
Winners of the Pro/Am were Graham Hawthorn, first place; Waes Kieser, second; and Jason Richards, third.
Josh Walters, one of the spectators at Saturday’s games, said his family’s Scottish heritage was a main reason he wanted to attend the event.
Walters said he enjoyed “watching the competitors compete against each other and try to do some of these competitions, because they are certainly not easy to do.”
Although Walters has not yet tried his hand at the games, he isn’t ruling it out.
“Not yet, but it could be possible in the future that I might be interested in doing so once I get some energy and stamina back,” he said.
Competitor Jen Gomez cited both health and heritage as factors that have contributed to her passion for competing in Highland Games.
“I started in this because I had lost a bunch of weight and I knew that strength training was the best way to, like, maintain muscle and maintain that weight loss,” she said.
Gomez, who described herself as “very Scottish,” said she attended the Central Carolina Highland Games four years ago.
“I watched a bunch of these ladies actually compete and I was like, ‘I bet I could do that,’ and then I got into it.”
Gomez said staying healthy is one of the main challenges a competitor faces.
“There’s a lot of ways you can get injured and I think truly it’s just the confidence to jump both feet in,” she said. “We’re a fun group. We want people to join in with us and a lot of people think that it is technique driven but we will get you there. It’s fun. We just want people to come out and join us.”
Gomez said she attended Central Carolina Highland Games four years ago after seeing it advertised on a billboard.
“I watched a bunch of my friends compete and I was like, ‘oh, I can do that with them.’ It’s been really cool.”
Alyssa Cannonwood, who took part in the Historical European Martial Arts sword fighting at the event, said she started fencing in high school.
“And so it was kind of a natural progression from Olympic style fencing into HEMA over the last four or five years,” Cannonwood said. “And the leadership team for the club was like, ‘hey, we’re looking at doing a fencing tournament. Anybody want to participate?’”
She said the sport is fun.
“We like hitting each other with swords,” Cannonwood said.
She said the club has been doing mock tournaments, which helped her prepare for Saturday.
“So I’m part of Triangle Sword Guild and we’ve been doing Monday night kind of sparring matches,” Cannonwood said. “So we’ll do match-ups between various people of various skill levels. We’re doing judge training as well to make sure that the team judging the event is all capable and know what they’re doing. So we’ve been doing that for a good few months and, you know, kind of just came in ready to go and have a good time.”
Cannonwood encouraged anyone interested in sword fighting to find a club near them. Triangle Sword Guild will be the closest club for most area residents, she said.
“And just show up to the first class,” she said. “You don’t need anything. Just come. Be ready to have fun. You don’t have to be super-athletic. You know, you’ll get there eventually. It’s a very open, welcoming community. So just show up.”
In addition to the athletic competitions, the event also includes traditional Scottish music, food and craft vendors.
